description_full: Allegion plc engages in the provision of security products and solutions worldwide. It is operating through two segments: Allegion Americas and Allegion International. The company offers door controls, door control system, and exit devices; doors, glass and door systems, and accessories; electronic security products and access control systems, including time, attendance, and workforce productivity; and locks, locksets, portable locks, and key systems. It also provides services and software, such as inspection, maintenance, and repair services for its automatic entrance solutions; software as a service, including access control, platform integration, and workforce management solutions; and ongoing aftermarket services, and design and installation offerings. In addition, the company sells its products and solutions to end-users in commercial, institutional, and residential facilities, including education, healthcare, government, hospitality, retail, commercial office, and single and multi-family residential markets under the CISA, Interflex, LCN, Schlage, SimonsVoss, and Von Duprin brands. It sells its products and solutions through distribution and retail channels, such as specialty distribution, e-commerce, and wholesalers, as well as through various retail channels comprising do-it-yourself home improvement centers, online and e-commerce platforms, and small specialty showroom outlets. Allegion plc was incorporated in 2013 and is based in Dublin, Ireland.

financial_summary: Allegion plc is a large-cap industrials business with a $16.3B market cap on $4.1B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +8% over the past three years and +7% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 23% against a 8% cost of capital — a 14-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat.

The business throws off $686M in free cash flow — roughly 17 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.22× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.6× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 8.5×.

Shareholder yield is only 1.6%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 1.9× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sector_headwinds.text: Low reinvestment-driven growth suggests the compounding engine has stalled
Trading near 52-week highs — the market has already recognised the story (confirmed by 1 other valuation measure)
Insiders are net sellers (89% sell ratio, net $3.8M) — the people closest to the business are reducing their personal stake
Significant goodwill (37% of assets) from past acquisitions — a soft asset a conservative appraisal discounts to zero
Industrials sector lagging the market significantly, underperforming by 6% over 3 months
Cyclicality and capital intensity — order books turn on a dime, and the heavy fixed cost base that creates the moat also magnifies the downturn.
Supply chain reshoring costs and labour shortages — onshoring mandates raise capex requirements while a shrinking skilled-labour pool inflates operating costs.
Tariff and trade-policy exposure — industrial exporters sit squarely in the crosshairs of protectionist policy, and retaliatory tariffs can close markets without warning.

sector_tailwinds: Operating margins 12% above sector median — the quantitative trace of pricing power
Returns on capital have been remarkably steady for 5 years — durability is the real test of a moat
Altman Z comfortably in the safe zone — a fortress balance sheet on this measure
12 consecutive years of dividend payments — an operating record that makes the dividend claim credible
Healthy payout ratio leaves room for both dividend growth and reinvestment
ROIC sits in the top quartile of Industrials peers — the moat is wider than the neighbourhood

sect: Its 21% operating margin runs 12pp above the Industrials median (9%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 1.90x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
It accounts for 0.1% of sector revenue and 0.2% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+3.6% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 548 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted lower, down 6% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has rebounded 15% over the last three months.
The price sits near the top of its 52-week range, 2% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 30% and a beta of 0.85, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.00 vs 5y 0.81), so read it loosely.
Liquidity is deep, with about $164.7M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 43% in the 2020 crash and 32% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $186 (margin of safety -3%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 13%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $145 to $243 (P10-P90).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 30% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 4.2% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 4.8% (vs the 8% bar).
The 11 covering analysts target $194 on average, 1% above the price.
The price implies 8.7% annual cash-flow growth.
prof: ROIC of 23% clears the cost of capital of 8.4% by 14pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have been steady (CV 0.12).
It converts 17% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.22x.
ROE of 31% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.5x equity multiplier).
It spends 3.2% of revenue on R&D and 0.7% on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 1.6x net debt to EBITDA ($356.2M of cash against $2.0B of debt), above the 1.5x gate, with interest covered 8.5x.
Goodwill makes up 37% of assets, a soft asset exposed to impairment.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 7.5% over 3 years, 8.4% over 5 years and 7.0% over 10 years.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 9.1% a year over five years.
Capex runs only 0.8x depreciation (2.4% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 25, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
Analysts expect 11.4% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.2%), and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Insider trading is two-way: 1 purchase and 8 sales over the past year, net $3.8M sold.
Shareholder yield is a modest 1.6% (0.5% in buybacks and 1.1% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 0.9% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 12 consecutive years, raising it 8.4% a year over the last five.
people: With about 13,300 employees, each generates about $306K of revenue, 0.8x the Industrials median, and revenue has grown 6.1% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $52K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $3.1M (10x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (3/10, lower is better).
